title: CancellationToken in consumers (cooperative shutdown)
hook: CancellationToken is a cooperative flag plus callbacks. Queue and HTTP shutdown only works if every await observes the same token the host cancelled.

blocks.text: CancellationToken is a lightweight struct that views a CancellationTokenSource. When Cancel is called, IsCancellationRequested becomes true and registered callbacks fire. It does not abort a thread — cancellation is cooperative. HttpClient, StackExchange.Redis, and AWS SDK calls that accept a token will complete early or throw OperationCanceledException. A tight CPU loop must call ThrowIfCancellationRequested itself.

entries.plainDefinition: A struct that signals whether cancellation has been requested. Pass it into async methods.
The object that owns the cancellation state. Call Cancel() to signal all linked tokens.
Combines multiple tokens. Cancels when any parent token cancels.
The operation must check the token. A library that never observes it will keep running.

blocks.text: For a queue consumer, the generic host's StoppingToken is the process lifetime. Pass it into the receive loop. When Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, you stop fetching, finish or nack the in-flight message according to policy, then exit before the grace period. Catching OperationCanceledException and treating it as a poison message during deploy is a common production bug. Link host lifetime tokens with per-operation timeouts so a hung receive does not block shutdown.

blocks.title: Ack vs nack on cancellation
blocks.body: If stoppingToken fires mid-handle, requeue when work is idempotent. Drop or send to a dead-letter queue when a partial side effect already committed. Never ignore the token in a Redis SET that is part of the same unit of work you will retry.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Host provides StoppingToken
items.body: The generic host or Kubernetes signals shutdown via CancellationToken.

items.title: Pass token into receive loop
items.body: Every ReceiveAsync, HTTP call, and Redis operation receives the same token.

items.title: Link with per-operation timeout
items.body: CreateLinkedTokenSource combines host shutdown with a 25-second receive timeout.

items.title: Catch and distinguish
items.body: OperationCanceledException when stoppingToken fired = graceful exit. Timeout alone = retry the receive.

diagram.title: Token linking for consumer shutdown
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  H[Host StoppingToken] --> L[CreateLinkedTokenSource]
  T[CancelAfter 25s timeout] --> L
  L --> R[ReceiveAsync with linked token]
  R --> C{Which token fired?}
  C -->|StoppingToken| S[Break loop — graceful shutdown]
  C -->|Timeout only| G[Continue — retry receive]
  C -->|Neither| P[Process message]

snippet.label: SQS loop with host token and per-message timeout
snippet.explanation: Linked tokens expire a hung receive without treating host shutdown and a 25-second timeout as the same condition.

snippet.label: ThrowIfCancellationRequested in a CPU loop
snippet.explanation: Async I/O methods observe the token automatically. CPU loops must check explicitly between iterations.

snippet.label: Register callback for non-async resources
snippet.explanation: token.Register runs a callback when cancellation fires. Useful for resources that do not have built-in token support.

snippet.label: Failure mode: treating shutdown as poison
snippet.explanation: During Kubernetes rolling deploy, StoppingToken fires. Catching it as a generic Exception and nacking wastes messages and triggers false poison alerts.

blocks.title: CancellationToken vs AbortController
rows: Pass token to every async call
Pass signal to fetch and friends

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Catching Exception and nacking cancellation as a poison message during deploy. Forgetting to pass the token into nested Redis and HTTP calls. Leaking CancellationTokenSource instances in a high-throughput loop. Passing CancellationToken.None in a public library method unless the operation truly cannot stop.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: during a Kubernetes rolling deploy, watch whether in-flight SQS messages get nacked as poison when StoppingToken fires — that is a cancellation-handling bug, not a message failure. Use IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping to trace token propagation. Linked sources with CancelAfter prevent a hung Receive from blocking shutdown past the grace period. CancellationTokenSource implements IDisposable — leak them in a tight loop and gen-2 grows.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Must pass to every await in the loop
Do not confuse with host shutdown
Callback must be thread-safe and fast

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying cancellation is preemptive like Thread.Abort — it is cooperative; the code must observe the token. Nacking a message as poison when OperationCanceledException fires during deploy. Not linking host token with per-receive timeout — a hung receive blocks shutdown. Creating a new CancellationTokenSource per message without disposing it.

interviewTakeaways: CancellationToken is a cooperative flag — nothing stops until code checks the token or passes it to an await.
Link host StoppingToken with per-operation CancelAfter so hung receives do not block SIGTERM grace period.
In production, distinguish OperationCanceledException from host shutdown versus timeout-only when deciding ack versus nack.

60s: Cancellation is cooperative. Pass host token to every await. Link with timeout via CreateLinkedTokenSource. Catch OperationCanceledException separately. Dispose linked sources. Never nack deploy cancellation as poison.
Follow-up: what happens to an in-flight HTTP call when StoppingToken fires mid-request?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'Cancel() aborts the thread' gets you rejected — cancellation is cooperative, not preemptive.
Catching Exception and nacking cancellation as poison during deploy — treats graceful shutdown as failure.
Strong answer: 'I pass StoppingToken through the receive loop, link with timeout, catch OperationCanceledException separately, and dispose linked sources.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: AbortSignal is the JS cousin: fetch observes it, CPU loops must poll aborted. C# tokens also multicast to many operations through linked sources.
TypeScript 5.2+ adds AbortSignal.timeout(ms) — similar to CancellationTokenSource.CancelAfter. C# linking multiple tokens is more explicit with CreateLinkedTokenSource.
